title: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021)
summary: Only the class members with the relevant concrete injury could recover damages in federal court; the Court distinguished inaccurate files from disseminated reports.
notes:
The assigned note expressly states that the Court did not decide whether every class member must establish standing before certification. Preserve that reservation.

Justice Kavanaugh wrote for a 5–4 Court (Roberts, Alito, Gorsuch, Barrett joining); the opinion's rule is often reduced to "No concrete harm, no standing," and it held that only plaintiffs concretely harmed by a statutory violation may seek damages against a private defendant in federal court.

sections.Parties: A class of consumers sued TransUnion under the Fair Credit Reporting Act over misleading information in their credit files.
sections.Material Facts: TransUnion had associated the consumers with a government list of specially designated nationals, which included terrorists and other persons presenting national-security concerns. The class contained 8,185 consumers, but the parties stipulated that reports concerning only 1,853 had been disseminated to potential creditors during the relevant period. The remaining 6,332 files had not been provided to third parties in that period. The class alleged failures of reasonable accuracy procedures and required disclosures.
sections.Procedural History: The district court certified the class, and the jury awarded statutory and punitive damages. The Ninth Circuit reduced the punitive award but found standing for the class. The Supreme Court reversed the standing determination in part and remanded for reconsideration of certification.
sections.Issue: Did all class members have Article III standing to recover individual damages because their statutory rights were violated?
sections.Holding: No. The majority found concrete reputational harm for the disseminated reports and insufficient concrete harm for the undisseminated files on the theory before it.
sections.Reasoning: The majority required the parties invoking federal jurisdiction to show the injury that Article III demands. A class-action device cannot confer a damages remedy on a person who lacks that jurisdictional injury. Dissemination supplied the concrete reputational harm relevant here; the inaccurate internal files did not establish the same harm merely by existing. The Court distinguished Congress’s creation of a statutory cause of action from the constitutional conditions of federal adjudication.

learning.why: Only the class members with the relevant concrete injury could recover damages in federal court; the Court distinguished inaccurate files from disseminated reports.

topics.cp-standing: Every class member recovering individual damages needed a concrete injury satisfying Article III.
topics.cp-class-jurisdiction: Class certification did not automatically supply standing for uninjured members.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: A statutory violation and an Article III injury were distinct questions in the majority’s analysis.
topics.cp-article-iii: The holding rests on the Article III case-or-controversy requirement and the limits on Congress's power to confer standing by statute.
topics.cp-class-certification: The Court held every class member must have standing to recover damages and remanded for reconsideration of certification, flagging the open typicality question about Ramirez.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Thomas, joined by Justices Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan, dissented, arguing that a violation of an individualized private right created by Congress has historically sufficed as injury in fact. Justice Kagan, joined by Justices Breyer and Sotomayor, also filed a separate dissent. The majority opinion was by Justice Kavanaugh for a 5–4 Court.

LRS.title: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez
LRS.summary: The statutory existence of a cause of action did not eliminate the need to establish concrete and particularized harm.

sections.Parties: Individuals asserted claims against TransUnion under the Fair Credit Reporting Act.
sections.Material Facts: The dispute included plaintiffs claiming violations of a statutory consumer-reporting right. The assigned note focuses on whether those violations caused concrete harm and does not reproduce the underlying reporting records or dissemination facts.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court held that some plaintiffs lacked Article III standing.
sections.Issue: How courts assess the concreteness of asserted statutory injuries when Congress has authorized a lawsuit.
sections.Holding: Congressional recognition of an interest is instructive, but a plaintiff must still show concrete and particularized injury. Some plaintiffs in the case lacked it.
sections.Reasoning: The Court looked for a close relationship between the alleged harm and harms traditionally recognized as supporting suit. Physical and economic harms qualify; intangible harms such as reputational injury, disclosure of private information, and intrusion can also qualify. Congress may elevate existing real-world harm into an actionable injury, but cannot create Article III injury merely by calling a harmless event actionable. This source supports that framework, not a detailed account of every affected TransUnion class member.
